    18	The geometric line carrier records the sampled coordinate, and line evaluation
    19	uses an `Option` outcome rather than assigning a value when a point does not
    20	determine one.  The game retains the point, axis-line, and diagonal-line answer
    21	formats and the nine ordered type branches of the original low-degree game.
    22	
    23	The `Transport` modules relate the direct game to the seed-indexed game and to
    24	the low individual degree test: `Transport.Correspondence`
    25	identifies coordinates, answers, and the question law of the two QPBT
    26	presentations; `Transport.SeedFiber` dilates a seed-indexed strategy to a
    27	direct strategy by a correlated residue register, and `Transport.SeedFiberValue`
    28	shows that the dilation preserves the value exactly; `Transport.Questions`
    29	reads LDT lines as canonical direct questions and rebases direct answers;
    30	`Transport.Strategy` reads one coordinate of a projective direct strategy as a
    31	LDT projective strategy, with exact Born-weight formulas for both constructions;
    32	`Transport.Consistency` reexpresses the three single-polynomial LDT consistency
    33	relations in direct coordinates, the first two at a fixed tuple coordinate; and
    34	`Transport.BranchComparison`, `Transport.DiagonalRecursion`, and
    35	`Transport.PassConversion` convert a value bound of the direct game into the
    36	pass hypothesis of the low individual degree theorem for every
    37	coordinate strategy.  `GameValue` supplies the rejection calculus relating the
    38	direct value to the LDT branch weights.  `Transport.Error` carries the
    39	scalar half of the transport: the auxiliary sampling parameter with which
    40	the low individual degree theorem is applied, bounds on the three terms of its error
    41	function, and the absorption of the resulting simultaneous-measurement
    42	estimate into the error function of `lem:ld-soundness`.

   875	\section{Expanding the Hilbert space and defining commuting observables}
   876	\label{sec:expanding}
   877	
   878	The next step of the analysis adjoins ancillary EPR registers to the
   879	players' state and lifts the strategy observables and measurements to the
   880	expanded state. The point of the construction is that the ancilla factor of
   881	each lifted observable carries the \emph{exact} Pauli commutation sign, so
   882	that the signs cancel and the lifted observables approximately commute for
   883	every tuple $\omega$.

blueprint/src/chapter/ch16_qpbt_extraction.tex:71:	The source states the constructions of this chapter in terms of its boolean decoding map (the case $H = \{0,1\}$ of Definition~\ref{def:decoding-map}) while describing that map as returning the string of \emph{all} evaluations of $g$ on the hypercube. The proofs require the latter reading, $H = \F_q$, which is adopted throughout this chapter: the linearity of $\mathrm{Dec}$ and the identity $\mathrm{Dec}(g_h) = h$ for all $h \in \F_q^{M}$, both of which fail for the boolean map, are used in the symmetry step of the proof of Lemma~\ref{lem:qld-construct-the-paulis}. The source further asserts the identity $\mathrm{Dec}(g) \cdot \mathrm{ind}_m(u) = g(u)$ for every $g \in \mathrm{ideg}_{d,m}(\F_q)$. Since the left-hand side equals $g_{\mathrm{Dec}(g)}(u)$, the identity, taken for all $u \in \F_q^m$, states that the multilinear representative $g_{\mathrm{Dec}(g)}$ and $g$ induce the same function on $\F_q^m$. Every encoding satisfies it, because then $g_{\mathrm{Dec}(g)} = g$ as polynomial representatives; a polynomial that is not an encoding need not: for $m = 1$, $d \geq 2$, and $q > 2$, the polynomial $g(x) = x^2$ has $\mathrm{Dec}(g) \cdot \mathrm{ind}_1(u) = u$, which differs from $g(u) = u^2$ at every $u \notin \{0,1\}$. When $d \leq q-1$ the failure at some $u$ characterizes the polynomials that are not encodings, since evaluation is injective on representatives of individual degree at most $q-1$ (Definition~\ref{def:polynomials-degree}); when $d \geq q$ it does not: for the admissible tuple $(q,m,d) = (8,1,8)$, the polynomial $g(x) = x^8$ is not an encoding, yet $\mathrm{Dec}(g) \cdot \mathrm{ind}_1(u) = u = u^8 = g(u)$ for every $u \in \F_8$. Accordingly, the proofs below invoke the identity only for encodings; in the proof of Lemma~\ref{lem:qld-construct-the-paulis} the contribution of the remaining outcomes is controlled by the bound \eqref{eq:qld-nonencoding-mass} on the mass that the measurement of Lemma~\ref{lem:qld-4-7} places on polynomials that are not encodings, while in the conjugation identity \eqref{eq:qld-unitary-6} the quantity $\mathrm{Dec}(g) \cdot \mathrm{ind}_m(u)$ cancels exactly.

Replacing $(\tau^W_h)_{\mathrm{B}''}$ by the averaged coarse-graining $\E_u \sum_{h' : g_{h'}(u) = g_h(u)} (\tau^W_{h'})_{\mathrm{B}''}$ costs at most $md/q$ by Lemma~\ref{lem:schwartz-zippel-total-degree} (distinct $h \neq h'$ have distinct encodings $g_h \neq g_{h'}$, of total degree at most $md$), and by \eqref{eq:qld-unitary-6} the resulting sum equals $\E_u \sum_{a} \bra{\Delta} V_{\mathrm{A}} M^{(\mathrm{Pauli},W)}_{[g_h(u)=a]} V_{\mathrm{A}}^\dagger \ot V_{\mathrm{B}} \tilde{M}^{W,\mathrm{ind}_m(u)}_a V_{\mathrm{B}}^\dagger \ket{\Delta}$.    681	\label{sec:combining}
   682	
   683	In this section our goal is to create a set of combined measurements
   684	that simultaneously measure the approximately-commuting measurements
   685	constructed in the previous section. We do this first for the points.
   686	Recall that $\mH_\alice$ and $\mH_\bob$ denote the Hilbert spaces corresponding to
   687	registers $\alice$ and $\bob$, respectively.
   688	
   689	\begin{lemma}\label{lem:qld-4-10}
   690	There exists a function $\delta_Q(\eps) = \poly(\eps)$ such that the following holds. 
   691		For every $x,z \in \F_q^m$ and $\mH \in \{ \mH_\alice, \mH_\bob\}$ there are projective measurements $\{ \hat{Q}^{x,z}_{a,b} \}_{a,b \in \F_q}$ acting on $\mathcal{H} \otimes (\C^q)^{\otimes \nqubits}$ such that:
   692		\begin{enumerate}
   693			\item (\textbf{Self-consistency}) On average over uniformly random $x,z \in \F_q^m$,
   694			\begin{equation}
   695				\label{eq:qld-q-self-cons}
   696				(\hat{Q}^{x,z}_{a,b})_{\alice \alice'}  \approx_{\delta_Q} (\hat{Q}^{x,z}_{a,b})_{\bob \alice''}\,.
   697			\end{equation}
   698			
   699			\item (\textbf{Consistency with $\hat{M}$}) On average over uniformly random $x,z \in \F_q^m$,
   700			\begin{gather}
   701				\label{eq:qld-q-cons-m-hat-xz}
   702					(\hat{Q}^{x,z}_{a,b})_{\alice \alice'} \approx_{\delta_Q} (\hat{M}^{(\Point,X),x}_{a} \hat{M}^{(\Point,Z),z}_b)_{\bob \alice''}\;, \\
   703								\label{eq:qld-q-cons-m-hat-zx}
   704					(\hat{Q}^{x,z}_{a,b})_{\alice \alice'} \approx_{\delta_Q} (\hat{M}^{(\Point,Z),z}_b  \hat{M}^{(\Point,X),x}_{a} )_{\bob \alice''}\;.
   705			\end{gather}
   706	              \end{enumerate}
   707	                    Furthermore, all symmetric equivalents of these approximations
   708	      also hold.
   709	\end{lemma}
   710	
   711	The construction of the measurements $\{ \hat{Q}^{x,z}_{a,b} \}$ whose existence is guaranteed in the lemma proceeds in three steps. In the first step, for every $(r,s)\in\F_q^2$ we combine the binary-outcome measurements $\hat{M}^{(\Point,X),x,r}_a$ and $\hat{M}^{(\Point,X),z,s}_b$; this is made possible by their approximate commutation as shown in Lemma~\ref{lem:qld-comm-cons}. In a second step, we show that the measurements thus constructed have a particular ``approximate linearity'' property, when seen as a function of the pair $(r,s)$. This allows us, in the third step, to combine them into a single measurement $\{ \hat{Q}^{x,z}_{a,b} \}$ with outcomes in $\F_q^2\cong \F_2^{2t}$ by applying the following  result from~\cite{NV17}:
   712		
   713		\begin{theorem}[Quantum linearity test]
   714		\label{thm:linearity}
   715			Let $0 \leq \delta \leq 1$, let $t$ be a positive integer, and let $\ket{\psi}$ be a state in a Hilbert space $\mathcal{H}_\alice \otimes \mathcal{H}_\bob$. Let $\{\mathcal{O}^u \}$ be a set of observables indexed by $u \in \F_2^t$ that act on $\mathcal{H}_\alice$. Suppose that on average over $u, u'$ chosen uniformly from $\F_2^t$, we have the following ``approximate linearity'' holds:
   716			\[
   717	(\mathcal{O}^u \mathcal{O}^{u'})_{\alice} \approx_\delta (\mathcal{O}^{u+u'})_{\alice}
   718			\]
   719			where the $\approx$ statement is taken with respect to the state $\ket{\psi}$. 
   720	Then there exists an extended state $\ket{\psi'}_{\alice \alice' \bob} = \ket{\psi}_{\alice \bob} \otimes \ket{0}_{\alice'}$ in an extended space $\mathcal{H}_{\alice} \otimes \mathcal{H}_\bob \otimes \mathcal{H}_{\alice'}$ and observables $\{ \mathcal{L}^u \}$ acting on $\mathcal{H}_\alice \otimes \mathcal{H}_{\alice'}$ such that for all $u, u' \in \F_2^t$, 
   721			\[
   722				\mathcal{L}^u \mathcal{L}^{u'} = \mathcal{L}^{u + u'} \qquad \text{and} \qquad (\mathcal{L}^u)_{\alice \alice'} \approx_\delta (\mathcal{O}^u)_\alice \,.
   723			\]
   724			Furthermore, the observable $\mathcal{L}^u = \Id$ when $u = 0$.
   725		\end{theorem}

   455	\begin{remark}[Two steps in the source proof of the extraction lemma]\label{rem:qld-unitary-triangle-slip}

     3	Key design patterns used in the MIPStarRE Lean formalization to bridge the
     4	gap between paper-level mathematics and a compilable Lean proof.
     5	
     6	This document is intended for contributors who need to understand *why* the
     7	Lean code is structured as it is, and for reviewers who need to recognize
     8	these patterns when reading PRs.  It complements the individual chapter audits
     9	in `audits/`, the proof-integrity rules in the lean-conventions skill (addenda:
    10	`docs/project_conventions.md`), and the
    11	proof-gap protocol in `docs/paper-gaps/proof-gap-protocol.tex`.
    12	
    13	## Table of Contents
    14	
    15	1. [Source-faithful statements and internal proof obligations](#pattern-1-source-faithful-statements-and-internal-proof-obligations)
    16	2. [Blueprint–Lean synchronization](#pattern-2-blueprintlean-synchronization)
    17	3. [Split-module architecture](#pattern-3-split-module-architecture)

    24	## Pattern 1: Source-faithful statements and internal proof obligations
    25	
    26	### The rule
    27	
    28	A declaration presented as the formalization of a paper theorem, lemma,
    29	proposition, or corollary must state the paper result, up to faithful formal
    30	encoding of the mathematical domain.  Its public hypotheses and conclusion are
    31	both part of the statement.  Adding a load-bearing bridge, residual, repair,
    32	obligation-structure input, hypotheses bundle, or assumptions bundle not present
    33	in the cited statement changes the theorem into a conditional helper.
    34	
    35	The project therefore distinguishes three objects.
    36	
    37	| Object | Public statement | Blueprint status |
    38	|--------|------------------|------------------|
    39	| Paper theorem | Matches the cited result in `references/ldt-paper/` | May be linked by source-labelled `\lean{}`; statement-level `\leanok` only when the statement matches |
    40	| Internal proof obligation | Proves a missing intermediate mathematical input from paper hypotheses | May contain a tracked `sorry` while the proof is open |
    41	| Conditional helper | Quarantines an unproved intermediate obligation | Not a paper theorem; no source-labelled `\leanok` |
    42	
    43	It is never allowed to change the public statement of a declaration presented
    44	as the formalization of a source-labelled paper theorem.  At the final assembly
    45	point, the paper theorem must either discharge the extra hypotheses internally,
    46	or remain as the paper-aligned statement with an unfinished proof while the
    47	conditional helper is given a different name.
    48	
    49	The preferred way to expose unfinished work is a named internal theorem or
    50	definition with a precise paper-origin docstring and, if necessary, a tracked
    51	`sorry`.  This makes the proof frontier visible without weakening the statement
    52	of a source-labelled theorem.
    53	
    54	### Why legacy scaffolding may remain temporarily
    55	
    56	| Temporary reason | Explanation |
    57	|------------------|-------------|
    58	| **Localizing an obstruction** | A conditional helper can isolate the exact missing mathematical input while the obligation discharger is being proved. |
    59	| **Recovering useful proof content** | The proof body may contain genuine estimates or constructions that should be extracted into source-faithful lemmas. |
    60	| **Auditability** | An explicit temporary hypothesis is easier to find than an implicit assumption hidden in prose, provided it is named as proof debt. |
    61	
    62	These reasons do not justify strengthening a paper theorem.  They only explain
    63	why a short-lived helper declaration may exist while its remaining hypotheses
    64	are being actively removed.
    65	
    66	### How to proceed when a proof needs an extra input
    67	
    68	1. **Check the source statement.**  Read the corresponding TeX in
    69	   `references/ldt-paper/` before changing a theorem linked from the blueprint.
    70	2. **Keep the paper-facing declaration source-faithful.**  Boundary hypotheses
    71	   such as positivity, nonemptiness, decidability, field-model instances, or
    72	   type-class assumptions may be faithful encodings when they are needed to
    73	   state the mathematics in Lean.  Proof data such as `BridgeInputs`,
    74	   `RepairInput`, `Residual`, `Package`, generic `Hypotheses`, or generic
    75	   `Assumptions` is different: it is not a paper assumption unless the cited
    76	   statement says so.
    77	3. **Name the missing intermediate result.**  If the proof uses a mathematical
    78	   fact not yet formalized, state it as a separate proof obligation.  A
    79	   temporary `sorry` in this declaration is preferable to adding the obligation as
    80	   a hypothesis on the paper theorem.
    81	4. **Do not introduce conditional helpers by default.**  A helper whose name
    82	   ends in `_ofObligations` is a quarantine device, not a normal formalization
    83	   pattern.  It may remain temporarily only when it preserves substantial proof
    84	   content that cannot yet be connected to the paper hypotheses, has a tracked
    85	   discharge or deletion target, and has no source-labelled blueprint
    86	   `\leanok`.  If the helper would merely package missing work as an extra
    87	   hypothesis, restore the theorem with the paper statement and leave a tracked
    88	   `sorry` instead.
    89	5. **Audit the final statement.**  Every PR touching a source-labelled theorem
    90	   should compare paper assumptions and Lean assumptions, paper conclusion and
    91	   Lean conclusion, and report whether the Lean statement is exact, has only
    92	   faithful boundary hypotheses, or has extra assumptions.
    93	
    94	If a paper-facing declaration is temporarily proved by calling a conditional
    95	helper whose load-bearing input has not yet been produced from the paper
    96	hypotheses, the proof frontier must be marked explicitly.  The declaration
    97	should carry an `**Unfaithful:**` docstring section naming the non-paper
    98	dependency, citing the paper-gap note or tracking issue, and identifying the
    99	internal theorem that will remove the dependency.  A named proof obligation
   100	with a tracked `sorry` is preferred whenever possible, because it makes the
   101	missing mathematical assertion visible without adding it to the paper theorem
   102	statement.
   103	
   104	### Required metadata for new proof-obligation declarations
   105	
   106	A new declaration whose name contains a proof-debt token such as `Bridge`,
   107	`Residual`, `Repair`, `Package`, `Producer`, `Input`, `Hypotheses`,
   108	`Assumptions`, `Obligation`, or `Witness` must explain its mathematical role in
   109	the def-site docstring.  A paper citation alone is not enough, because the
   110	reviewer must be able to tell whether the declaration is part of the paper
   111	statement or a Lean-only proof obligation.
   112	
   113	Use one of the following markers.
   114	
   115	| Marker | Use |
   116	|--------|-----|
   117	| `**Source:**`, `**Paper source:**`, or `**Source statement:**` | The declaration is a faithful formal encoding of a cited source statement or a field of that statement |
   118	| `**Faithful encoding:**` | The declaration records boundary data or domain data that the paper uses implicitly |
   119	| `**Proof obligation:**` or `**Internal proof obligation:**` | The declaration is a theorem or record that must be proved from the paper hypotheses before a source theorem is complete |
   120	| `**Conditional:**` | The declaration is a conditional helper; it must not be linked as the source theorem |
   121	| `**Unfaithful:**` | The declaration or proof currently depends on a load-bearing assumption not yet derived from the paper hypotheses |
   122	
   123	Proof-obligation, conditional, and unfaithful markers must cite a paper-gap note
   124	or tracking issue and must state the planned discharge or elimination theorem.
   125	If such a declaration would merely package missing work as an added hypothesis
   126	to a source theorem, do not introduce it; restore the source theorem statement
   127	and leave the missing proof as a tracked `sorry`.
   128	
   129	### Conditional helper boundary
   130	
   131	1. **Prefer a source theorem with a tracked `sorry`.**  If a proof requires a
   132	   construction that is not yet available from the paper hypotheses, the first
   133	   repair is to restore the source theorem statement and leave the missing proof
   134	   open.  Do not introduce a new `Input`, `Obligation`, `Residual`, `Repair`,
   135	   `Producer`, or `Package` merely to avoid that `sorry`.
   136	
   137	2. **Do not bundle several missing theorem-level steps into one hypothesis.**
   138	   The former Section 9 bundle `SelfImprovementObligations` and the helper

   140	   helper strong self-consistency, orthonormalization, and final-field transport

   142	   boundary is now the theorem `selfImprovement`, whose missing
   143	   proof is an explicit `sorry`.
   144	
   145	   The former induction-section helper

   148	   constructors.  Those constructors now call the theorem

   152	3. **Propagation is a warning sign.**  The consumer of

    41	\section{Basic objects}
    42	
    43	\paragraph{Source theorem.}
    44	A source theorem is a theorem, lemma, proposition, or corollary in the paper
    45	source under \path{references/ldt-paper/}.  Its hypotheses and conclusion are
    46	the mathematical ground truth, subject only to faithful formal encoding and to
    47	documented paper-gap corrections.
    48	
    49	\paragraph{Paper-facing declaration.}
    50	A \Lean{} declaration is paper-facing when it is named or cited as the
    51	formalization of a source theorem, for instance through a blueprint
    52	\verb|\lean{}| link on a theorem environment carrying a paper label.  Such a
    53	declaration must match the source theorem in its public statement.  In
    54	particular, it may not add an unproved bridge, residual, repair, input,
    55	obligation structure, or other proof-obligation hypothesis which the paper does
    56	not assume.
    57	
    58	\paragraph{Proof obligation.}
    59	A proof obligation is an intermediate assertion needed by the proof of a source
    60	theorem.  It may be a construction, an estimate, a transport lemma, or a
    61	comparison between two formal representations.  If the paper proves or invokes
    62	this assertion, then the formalization should state it as a separate lemma or
    63	theorem and prove it from the upstream hypotheses.
    64	
    65	\paragraph{Obligation discharger.}
    66	An obligation discharger is a theorem or definition which constructs a proof
    67	obligation from the paper hypotheses already available at that point in the
    68	argument.  This is the preferred representation of missing work.  If the proof
    69	is not yet complete, the discharger may temporarily contain a tracked
    70	\verb|sorry|, but the paper-facing theorem should call it rather than assume
    71	its output as an additional theorem hypothesis.
    72	
    73	\paragraph{Conditional helper.}
    74	A conditional helper is a separately named theorem whose statement explicitly
    75	assumes a proof obligation.  Names such as
    76	\leanid{mainFormal\_ofInternalObligations},
    77	\leanid{orthonormalization\_ofInput}, or names whose suffix advertises the
    78	assumed obligation are permitted only when the declaration is not presented as
    79	the source theorem.  A conditional helper is a quarantine for downstream proof
    80	content; it does not close the source theorem.
    81	
    82	\section{Bridge, residual, repair, input, and obligation structures}
    83	
    84	The words \emph{bridge}, \emph{residual}, \emph{repair}, \emph{input}, and
    85	\emph{obligation structure} name possible formal shapes.  They become dangerous
    86	when their mathematical status is unclear or when their names make unproved
    87	data look like acceptable hypotheses of a source theorem.
    88	
    89	\paragraph{Bridge.}
    90	A bridge should be a transport theorem between two already defined
    91	mathematical forms: for example, a tensor-placement identity, a conversion
    92	between two equivalent consistency relations, or a statement translating a
    93	source object into a formal representation.  A bridge is harmless only after it
    94	is proved from previously available assumptions.  It becomes proof debt when it
    95	is assumed because the transport has not yet been proved.  It becomes theorem
    96	drift when the assumed bridge is added to a paper-facing theorem.
    97	
    98	\paragraph{Residual.}
    99	A residual is a named remainder after part of an argument has been performed.
   100	It is often a useful way to record the exact missing target after a completed
   101	construction.  A residual may appear as the conclusion of a helper theorem or
   102	as the input of a quarantined conditional helper.  It is not a permissible new
   103	assumption on a paper theorem unless the paper itself assumes that residual.
   104	
   105	\paragraph{Input.}
   106	An input is a named bundle of data or hypotheses consumed by a construction or
   107	conditional helper.  It is harmless only when each load-bearing field is either
   108	part of the source hypotheses or is produced by an earlier theorem.  It becomes
   109	proof debt when the bundle is merely assumed because the construction of its
   110	fields is missing.  It becomes theorem drift when such a bundle is added to the
   111	public statement of a source theorem.
   112	
   113	\paragraph{Repair.}
   114	A repair is a mathematical construction which replaces an approximate or
   115	partial object by a better object, usually with a quantitative estimate.  In
   116	the low individual degree test formalization, projectivization and
   117	orthonormalization repairs are genuine mathematical operations.  A repair
   118	should therefore appear as a construction or as a theorem discharging the
   119	corresponding obligation.  If a theorem assumes the output of the repair instead
   120	of constructing it, that theorem is conditional on the repair.
   121	
   122	\paragraph{Obligation structure.}
   123	An obligation structure is a record whose fields are the data and estimates
   124	needed by a later construction.  This is acceptable only as an internal target
   125	or as a hypothesis of a conditional helper.  Such a structure becomes statement
   126	drift if it is added to a paper-facing theorem instead of being constructed
   127	inside the proof.  The review question is whether every load-bearing field is
   128	proved from the source hypotheses or is explicitly tracked as a missing
   129	obligation.
   130	
   131	\section{The main failure mode}
   132	
   133	Suppose the paper proves
   134	\[
   135	  H \Longrightarrow C.
   136	\]
   137	During formalization, the proof may need an intermediate assertion \(B\).  The
   138	paper theorem should be represented as
   139	\[
   140	  H \Longrightarrow B \Longrightarrow C
   141	  \quad\text{inside the proof,}
   142	\]
   143	where \(B\) is obtained by a lemma or theorem from \(H\).  The following
   144	public statement is a different theorem:
   145	\[
   146	  H \land B \Longrightarrow C.
   147	\]
   148	It is not unsound in \Lean{}, but it is not the paper theorem.  It says that the
   149	conclusion follows if the missing bridge data is supplied.  Such a theorem is a
   150	conditional helper, even if its conclusion looks exactly like the paper's
   151	conclusion.
   152	
   153	This is the situation colloquially described as ``adding a bridge
   154	hypothesis''.  More precisely, an unproved intermediate step has been promoted
   155	from the proof body to the theorem's assumptions.  The correction is not to hide
   156	the hypothesis under a different structure name.  The correction is to keep a
   157	paper-facing theorem with the source statement and move the missing step to a
   158	named internal proof obligation.
   159	
   160	\section{Faithful boundary hypotheses}
   161	
   162	Not every extra formal hypothesis is a theorem drift.  Some hypotheses are
   163	faithful boundary conditions introduced by formal encoding.  Examples include
   164	nonnegativity needed for a real power, positivity needed to divide by a
   165	quantity, finiteness and nonemptiness of an index type, a field-model instance,
   166	or decidability instances required by \Lean{}.  Such hypotheses are acceptable
   167	when they express part of the mathematical ambient setting or make explicit a
   168	condition used implicitly in the paper.
   169	
   170	The distinction is load-bearing.  A faithful boundary hypothesis describes the
   171	domain in which the paper's objects live.  A proof-debt hypothesis supplies a
   172	mathematical step that the proof should derive.  If removing the hypothesis
   173	leaves an unproved construction or estimate from the paper proof, then the
   174	hypothesis is proof debt, not a boundary condition.
   175	
   176	\section{Definition drift and subtree repair}
   177	
   178	Definition drift is especially dangerous because it propagates.  If a
   179	definition is changed so that it no longer denotes the object in the paper,
   180	then every downstream theorem using that definition may continue to compile
   181	while proving statements about the wrong object.  Downstream theorem statements
   182	can then be repaired piecemeal, but the development remains unstable because
   183	the wrong definition is still upstream.
   184	
   185	When a definition mismatch is found, the repair should proceed by a subtree
   186	protocol.
   187	
   188	\begin{enumerate}
   189	  \item Identify the source object and the formal object precisely.
   190	  \item Freeze a source-faithful definition or state an adapter theorem
   191	  relating the existing definition to the source object.
   192	  \item Recheck the downstream theorem chain against that definition or adapter.
   193	  \item Re-formalize the affected subtree from the corrected interface, rather
   194	  than adding local hypotheses to each downstream theorem.
   195	  \item If a downstream proof cannot be completed, record the missing obligation
   196	  at the lowest point where the paper proof needs it.
   197	\end{enumerate}
   198	
   199	This is slower than editing a final theorem signature, but it prevents a local
   200	definition error from becoming a global theorem-statement error.
   201	
   202	\section{Allowed shapes}
   203	
   204	\begin{center}
   205	\begin{tabular}{p{0.24\linewidth}p{0.31\linewidth}p{0.32\linewidth}}
   206	\textbf{Shape} & \textbf{Allowed use} & \textbf{Forbidden use} \\
   207	\hline
   208	Paper-facing theorem & Matches the source statement up to faithful encoding &
   209	Carries non-paper bridge, residual, repair, input, obligation-structure, or
   210	proof-obligation hypotheses \\
   211	Source-shaped theorem with a tracked \verb|sorry| & Default repair when the
   212	source proof is blocked but the statement is known & Replaced by a strengthened
   213	theorem statement merely to keep the file compiling \\
   214	Conditional helper & Temporary quarantine for substantial proof content whose
   215	remaining named obligation has not yet been discharged & Introduced merely to
   216	avoid a \verb|sorry|, or linked as the source theorem or marked as
   217	proof-complete for that theorem \\
   218	Obligation discharger theorem & Constructs the obligation from paper hypotheses &
   219	Merely restates the obligation as an assumption \\
   220	Input bundle & Collects produced data for a local construction & Is assumed by a
   221	source theorem instead of being produced \\
   222	Obligation structure & Bundles constructed data and estimates & Hides unproved
   223	fields that are then assumed by a source theorem \\
   224	Paper-gap note & Documents a real mathematical or formal-statement divergence &
   225	Justifies silent statement drift without a repair plan
   226	\end{tabular}
   227	\end{center}
   228	
   229	\section{Protocol for a blocked proof}
   230	
   231	When a source-labelled proof is blocked, use the following order.
   232	
   233	\begin{enumerate}
   234	  \item Read the cited source statement and the proof passage in
   235	  \path{references/ldt-paper/}.
   236	  \item Write the paper theorem form, the current \Lean{} theorem form, and the
   237	  first missing intermediate assertion.
   238	  \item Decide whether the missing assertion is a faithful boundary condition,
   239	  a representation adapter, an ordinary lemma from the paper proof, or a real
   240	  paper-gap discrepancy.
   241	  \item If it is an ordinary lemma or adapter, create a named theorem which
   242	  discharges that obligation.  Do not add it to the source theorem as a new
   243	  hypothesis.
   244	  \item Keep the source-labelled theorem itself in the source form, even if its
   245	  proof must contain a tracked \verb|sorry|.  This is the default repair when
   246	  the missing assertion has not yet been proved.
   247	  \item Create a conditional helper only to quarantine substantial proof content
   248	  that already exists and would otherwise be lost.  Do not create such a helper
   249	  merely to avoid a \verb|sorry| or to keep making progress.  If a conditional
   250	  helper remains, give it a conditional name, keep it separate from the
   251	  paper-facing theorem, and record the obligation discharger that must eliminate
   252	  it.
   253	  \item If the source and formal statements genuinely differ, write or update a
   254	  note under \path{docs/paper-gaps/} before marking the statement as aligned.
   255	  \item Update the blueprint so that paper labels point only to paper-facing
   256	  declarations.  Conditional helpers belong in remarks or implementation
   257	  notes, not in the source theorem block.
   258	\end{enumerate}
   259

blueprint/src/chapter/ch13_qpbt_test.tex:6:This chapter defines the two testing primitives underlying the question-reduction step: the \emph{classical low individual degree game}, in its simultaneous form, and the \emph{Pauli basis test}, a nonlocal game built from the classical game together with the Magic Square game. We state the quantum soundness of the classical game (Theorem~\ref{lem:ld-soundness}, imported, with the facts required by the identification, which remain to be proved, recorded in \cite{gap:qpbt_ld-dimension-divisibility}; see Remark~\ref{rem:ld-soundness-provider}), the rigidity of the Magic Square game (Theorem~\ref{thm:ms-rigidity}, imported), completeness of the Pauli basis test (Lemma~\ref{lem:pauli-completeness}), and the main soundness theorem for the Pauli basis test (Theorem~\ref{thm:pauli}), whose proof occupies Chapters~\ref{chap:qpbt-observables}--\ref{chap:qpbt-extraction} and is completed in Chapter~\ref{chap:qpbt-extraction} only modulo the proof obligation documented in \cite{gap:qpbt_ld-dimension-divisibility}. # Mathematical Language Guidelines

MIPStarRE Lean names and documentation should be written for readers comparing
the formalization with the paper and blueprint.

This is a project-local supplement to the Mathlib-derived documentation,
naming, and style guides in the lean-conventions skill's `MATHLIB_doc`,
`MATHLIB_naming`, and `MATHLIB_style` references.

## Scope

These guidelines apply to:

- public Lean declaration names and namespace names;
- module docstrings;
- declaration docstrings;
- documentation-visible section comments;
- explanatory comments that describe the mathematical role of a declaration.
- blueprint prose and formalization-support notes;
- issue titles and issue bodies;
- PR titles and PR descriptions.

## Source of Truth

Use terminology from the following sources, in this order:

1. `references/ldt-paper/`
2. `blueprint/src/chapter/`
3. established local conventions in nearby Lean files

When the paper has a term for the object, use that term. For Section 5, for
example, prefer orthogonalization lemma, truncation function, rounding to
projectors, rank reduction, and completing to measurement.

## Reference Notation And Terminology

The notation and terminology of the original reference are the default for
reader-facing mathematical text.  A reader should be able to compare a Lean
docstring, blueprint paragraph, issue, or PR description with the cited source
without first learning a private vocabulary used by the formalization.

When Lean must use a different name or representation, define the deviation in a
location which future readers can find from the affected statement.  Use the
first applicable location in the following order:

1. the declaration docstring of the public object whose name or representation
   differs from the paper;
2. the module docstring of the defining Lean file, when the deviation concerns a
   family of declarations in that file;
3. the relevant blueprint paragraph, when the notation appears only in the
   blueprint;
4. a report under `docs/reports/` or `docs/paper-gaps/`, when the deviation is a
   larger discrepancy between the paper, blueprint, and Lean.

The explanation should say:

- the notation or term used in the paper;
- the Lean object or name which represents it;
- the mathematical reason for the difference, if there is one;
- the scope in which the replacement should be used.

A PR description may mention the deviation, but it should not be the only place
where future readers can learn it.

Formalization-only auxiliary lemmas should be introduced as such.  Their prose
should name the nearby paper equation, theorem, or construction they support,
rather than presenting the auxiliary name as paper terminology.

## Naming Norm

Names and prose should describe the mathematical object, hypothesis, or
conclusion. They should not encode the history of how the formalization was
assembled.

Avoid presenting words such as `pipeline`, `wrapper`, `package`, `raw`,
`oneShot`, or `liveBlock` as mathematical terminology unless the cited source
uses them with that meaning. Likewise, avoid implementation-local substitutes
such as `projectivization` or `spectral truncation` when the paper gives a
clearer phrase.

This is a general rule for the repository, not only a rule for file splits.
Module names, namespace names, public declarations, theorem fields, docstrings,
blueprint-facing names, issue titles, and spec documents should name the
mathematical layer under discussion, not the local workflow step, paper line
number, or implementation history.

### Concrete examples

The table below illustrates the naming norm with examples patterned on the
codebase and on names seen during review.  Some entries are existing names;
others are proposed names for future refactors.  The "avoid" column lists
process-shaped names that encode the history of how the formalization was
assembled; the "prefer" column lists mathematical names that a reader of the
paper or blueprint would recognize.

| Avoid (process-shaped)                        | Prefer (mathematical)                     | Rationale                                              |
|:----------------------------------------------|:------------------------------------------|:-------------------------------------------------------|
| `Line130`                                     | `ProjectiveConsistency`                   | Paper Lemma 5.13, not "the line-130 identity"          |
| `Line169`                                     | `CompletionTransport`                     | Paper Lemma 5.16, step that transports completed data  |
| `Step6`                                       | `Orthonormalization`                      | Paper Section 5, the orthonormalization construction   |
| `FinalAssembly`                               | `DiagonalCompletion`                      | Paper Lemma 5.17, constructing a diagonal POVM         |
| `OneShotIneq`                                 | `SelfConsistencyDataProcessing` (or existing module `Preliminaries.SelfConsistency.DataProcessing`)           | Paper's data-processing inequality for self-consistency |
| `PipelineCheck`                               | `ErrorPropagationBound` (proposed)                   | The bound that propagates error through the test       |
| `QxpLayerWrapper`                             | `ProjectivePOVMCompletion` (proposed)                | The construction from round-projectors to POVMs        |
| `RawSpectralTruncation`                       | `SpectralTruncation`                      | The paper's spectral truncation, not an "unwrapped" version |
| `AddInUStep3To5`                              | `AddInUUpperExcessMass` (proposed)                  | Paper Addendum in §U, the upper excess-mass estimate   |
| `AddInUStep12`                                | `AddInUCommutationTail` (proposed)                   | Paper Addendum in §U, the commutation tail estimate    |

An avoided name is acceptable only when the cited paper itself uses that
phrase as the mathematical name (e.g., a lemma the paper calls "Step 2").
In that case the docstring should cite the paper's phrasing.

File-split PRs are a common place where this rule matters: new leaves should be
named by the mathematical boundary they isolate, and any public declarations
exposed by the split should be reviewed under the same standard.

### Shared helpers

When the same (or nearly the same) helper declaration appears in two or
more chapter-local leaves, the copies should be consolidated into a single
shared helper in an appropriate common module.  This avoids duplication and
ensures that fixes, generalizations, or upstream replacements apply to all
call sites at once.  Issue [#1145] tracks this work across the repository.

Procedure:

1. **Confirm equivalence.**  Compare the statement of each copy.  If the
   types differ only by a chapter-specific parameterization (e.g.,
   `SubMeas (Polynomial params) ι` vs `SubMeas (Point params) ι`),
   parameterize the shared helper over that type via a `variable` or
   explicit argument.
2. **Find the right home.**  Prefer a module that is already imported by
   both call sites.  Typical candidates:
   - `MIPStarRE/LDT/Basic/` for parameter-free operators and bounds,
   - `MIPStarRE/LDT/Preliminaries/` for polynomial/field/character lemmas,
   - The highest chapter that is a common dependency of the two sites.
3. **Name mathematically.**  Give the shared helper a name that describes
   what it states, not which chapter it originally came from.
4. **Replace call sites.**  Delete the chapter-local copies and replace
   their uses with the shared helper.  A thin wrapper is allowed only when it
   preserves a paper-facing or blueprint-facing name that external readers
   need to search for; such wrappers should have a docstring or compatibility
   comment explaining why the alias exists.  Remove the wrapper once that
   paper-facing name is no longer needed for external reference.
5. **Document.**  Add a docstring to the shared helper citing the paper or
   blueprint location it supports.

### Legacy identifier treatment

If a docstring must mention a legacy Lean identifier, cite it in backticks and
describe the mathematical object in paper terminology. If an old public
identifier cannot be renamed in the current PR, record the required migration
in the issue, PR description, or an audit file under `audits/`.

Do not add an empty pass-through abbreviation merely to introduce a second
public name.  This is different from a documented public wrapper allowed in the
shared-helper procedure above: a wrapper must preserve a paper-facing or
blueprint-facing term and must say why the alias exists.

## Review Checklist

Reviewers should use this checklist when examining public names and
documentation prose.  Flag any item that fails.

- [ ] **Naming.**  Do public declaration names, namespace names, module names,
      theorem field names, and docstring prose describe a mathematical object,
      hypothesis, or conclusion?  Or do they encode the history of how the
      formalization was assembled (paper line numbers, workflow steps,
      implementation-phase labels)?
- [ ] **Source alignment.**  For the mathematical content under review, does
      the prose use the terminology in `references/ldt-paper/` or the
      blueprint?  Are process words such as `pipeline`, `wrapper`, `package`,
      `raw`, `oneShot`, or `liveBlock` used as mathematical terms when the
      source does not use them that way?
- [ ] **Deviation documented.**  If a Lean name or representation differs from
      the paper, is the deviation documented in a declaration docstring,
      module docstring, blueprint paragraph, or `docs/paper-gaps/` note, in
      that order of preference?
- [ ] **Auxiliary lemmas.**  Are formalization-only auxiliary lemmas introduced
      as such, with prose naming the nearby paper equation, theorem, or
      construction they support?
- [ ] **Shared helpers.**  Does the PR introduce a helper that already exists
      (or near-exists) in another chapter-local leaf?  If so, has it been
      consolidated into a common module with a mathematical name?
- [ ] **Legacy IDs.**  If a legacy Lean identifier is mentioned, is the
      mathematical object described in paper terminology?  If an old public
      identifier cannot be renamed yet, is the required migration recorded in
      the issue, PR description, or an audit file?
- [ ] **Pass-through names.**  Does the PR add an empty pass-through
      abbreviation that introduces a second public name without adding
      mathematical content?  Reject it unless it is a documented compatibility
      wrapper preserving paper-facing or blueprint-facing terminology.

Review-fix PRs touching a surface covered by an active audit should read the
relevant audit before changing names or prose.

[#1145]: https://github.com/LionSR/MIPStarRE/issues/1145

   994		$T^{\ell_X,\ell_Z}_{f_X,f_Z}

   996		\hat{M}^{(\mathrm{Line},Z),\ell_Z}_{f_Z}

  1005		Lemma~\ref{lem:qld-4-10}. Applying

  1010		\approx_\delta
  1011		\sum_b (\hat{Q}^{x,z}_{a,b})_{\mathsf{A}\mathsf{A}'}
  1012		(\hat{M}^{(\mathrm{Point},Z),z}_{b})_{\mathsf{B}\mathsf{A}''}$,

  1014		\eqref{eq:qld-q-cons-m-hat-zx} yields the marginal consistencies

  1016		(\hat{M}^{(\mathrm{Point},X),x}_{a})_{\mathsf{B}\mathsf{A}''}$ and
  1017		$(\hat{Q}^{x,z}_{\bullet,b})_{\mathsf{A}\mathsf{A}'} \approx_{\delta_Q}

  1020		between $\approx$ and $\simeq$ with Lemma~\ref{fact:agreement} and
  1021		summing outcomes with Lemma~\ref{fact:data-processing}, the lines
  1022		measurements are consistent with the points measurements, and combining
  1023		with the marginal consistencies gives, on average over the line-point
  1024		distribution,
  1025		$(\hat{Q}^{x,z}_{a,\bullet})_{\mathsf{A}\mathsf{A}'} \simeq_{\delta_Q}
  1080		The combining map is also defined for polynomials restricted to lines.
  1081		Let $\ell$ be a line in $\F_q^{2m+2}$ with intercept
  1082		$u = (u_X, u_Z, u_\alpha, u_\beta)$ and slope
  1083		$v = (v_X, v_Z, v_\alpha, v_\beta)$, and let $\ell_X$ and $\ell_Z$ be
  1084		lines in $\F_q^m$ such that for every point
  1085		$(x, z, \alpha, \beta) \in \ell$ it holds that $x \in \ell_X$ and
  1086		$z \in \ell_Z$. Then for any two polynomials
  1087		$f \in \deg_{md}(\ell_X)$ and $g \in \deg_{md}(\ell_Z)$, the polynomial

  1089		\begin{equation}
  1090			\label{eq:combine-lines}
  1091			\mathrm{combine}_{f,g}(u + t \cdot v)
  1092			= (u_\alpha + t \cdot v_\alpha)\, f(u_X + t \cdot v_X)
  1093			+ (u_\beta + t \cdot v_\beta)\, g(u_Z + t \cdot v_Z)\,,
  1094			\qquad t \in \F_q\,.

  1097		polynomials of degree at most $md$ in the line parameter, and each is
  1098		multiplied by an affine factor of degree at most one.
  1099	\end{definition}

  1745	\begin{remark}[The error term in the source proof of
  1746		Lemma~\ref{lem:qld-4-13}]
  1747		\label{rem:qld-4-13-source-defects}
  1748		The statement of Lemma~\ref{lem:qld-4-13} retains the source error
  1749		form $\delta_{\mathrm{combine}} = \poly(m^2\eps, md/q)$, which
  1750		remains unproved. The source proof in \cite{Ji2020MIPStar} asserts
  1751		two different bounds for the quantity
  1752		\eqref{eq:qld-combined-lines-consistency}: the bound
  1753		$O(m(\eps^{1/4} + \delta_P^{1/4} + \delta_Q^{1/4} +
  1754		\delta_{\mathrm{Line}}^{1/2}))$, obtained by chaining the three
  1755		claims (Lemmas~\ref{lem:claim-17-1}--\ref{lem:claim-17-3}), and the
  1756		bound $O(m^2 \delta_P)$, whose derivation decomposes
  1757		\eqref{eq:qld-combined-lines-consistency} into
  1758		restricted-distribution terms bounded by
  1759		\eqref{eq:qld-xz-lines-restricted}. The second derivation requires a
  1760		joint product law for the pair $((\ell_X, x), (\ell_Z, z))$ that
  1761		Property~2 of Lemma~\ref{lem:qld-sublines} does not provide, and
  1762		neither bound is dominated by a function of $m^2\eps$ and $md/q$
  1763		alone that vanishes as its arguments vanish. The proof above
  1764		therefore follows the first route only and establishes the bound
  1765		$m \cdot \poly(\eps, md/q)$, which is the form consumed by
  1766		Lemma~\ref{lem:qld-4-7}, whose error function absorbs the prefactor
  1767		$m$ into $(md)^a$. The full analysis --- the two routes, the scalings
  1768		showing that the claimed form follows from neither, the corrected
  1769		deficit assertion in the proof of Lemma~\ref{lem:claim-17-2}, and the
  1770		candidate repairs with their open obligations --- is given in
  1771		\cite{gap:qpbt_combined-lines-error-term}.

   741	Since only admissible field sizes $q = 2^k$ arise in the Pauli basis test, the
   742	maximally entangled state $\ket{\mathrm{EPR}_q}$ and the qudit Pauli
   743	projectors are isomorphic to tensor products of qubit EPR states
   744	$\ket{\mathrm{EPR}_2}$ and qubit Pauli projectors. This is the content of the
   745	next lemma, which is what allows the Pauli basis test to self-test Pauli
   746	observables and maximally entangled states over \emph{qubits}
   747	(Chapter~\ref{chap:qpbt-test}).

   749	\begin{lemma}[Qudit-to-qubit isomorphism]\label{lem:pauli-binary}

   754		For all admissible field sizes $q = 2^k$ and integers $L \ge 0$, there
   755		exists an isomorphism $\phi : (\C^q)^{\ot L} \to (\C^2)^{\ot Lk}$ such that
   756		\begin{equation}\label{eq:epr-q-to-epr-2}

   759		\end{equation}
   760		(applying the natural identifications between
   761		$(\C^q)^{\ot L} \ot (\C^q)^{\ot L}$ and $(\C^q \ot \C^q)^{\ot L}$, and
   762		between $(\C^2)^{\ot Lk} \ot (\C^2)^{\ot Lk}$ and
   763		$(\C^2 \ot \C^2)^{\ot Lk}$). Moreover, for all $W \in \{X, Z\}$ and all
   764		$u \in \F_q^L$,
   765		\begin{equation}\label{eq:pauli-q-to-pauli-2}
   766			\tau^W_u = \phi^\dagger\,
   767			\Bigl(\bigotimes_{i=1}^L \bigotimes_{j=1}^k
   768			\sigma^W_{u_{ij}}\Bigr)\, \phi\;.
   769		\end{equation}

   771		$u_i = \sum_j u_{ij} e_j$ for all $i \in \{1, \dots, L\}$, where
   772		$\{e_1, \dots, e_k\}$ is the fixed self-dual normal basis of $\F_q$ over
   773		$\F_2$ of Definition~\ref{def:binary-representation}; and for
   774		$i \in \{1, \dots, L\}$ and $j \in \{1, \dots, k\}$ the $(i,j)$-th factor

   777		$s$-th qubit, where $s = (i-1)k + j$.
   778		We index the product coordinates from zero: values $(i-1,j-1)$ correspond to
   779		the paper's pair $(i,j)$.  The corrected upper bound $j\leq k$ is
   780		documented in \cite{gap:qpbt_pauli-binary-factor-index}.

/-!
# The quantum linearity theorem

This file proves the quantum linearity theorem of Natarajan and Vidick in the
form used to combine the binary observables produced in the point analysis.
A family of binary observables indexed by the Boolean cube `F_2^t`, whose
two-query linearity correlation weighted by a positive semidefinite trace-one
operator `ρ` is at least `1 - δ`, is close on average, in the state-dependent
distance weighted by `ρ ⊗ |anc⟩⟨anc|`, to an exactly linear family of binary
observables on a finite ancillary extension.

`avg_multiplicativeDefect_le_two_mul_error`, which converts the correlation
hypothesis into the bound `2δ` on the average multiplicative defect
`E_{u,u'} d_ρ(O^u O^{u'}, O^{u+u'})^2`, and Boolean representation stability
`exists_exact_boolean_representation`, which converts that defect bound into
the exactly linear family with the same average distance bound.  The notions
in which the theorem is stated are in

    32	/-- Parameters for the `(m,q,d)` low individual degree test.
    33	
    34	Besides the usual positivity assumptions, we bundle the paper-faithful witness

    36	structure Parameters where

    51	/-- Any number presented as a prime power is automatically positive. -/
    52	theorem q_pos_of_primePower {q : ℕ}
    53	    (hqPrimePower : ∃ p n, Nat.Prime p ∧ 0 < n ∧ q = p ^ n) : 0 < q := by
    54	  rcases hqPrimePower with ⟨p, n, hp, hn, rfl⟩
    55	  exact Nat.pow_pos hp.pos
    56	
    57	/-- Prime numbers are prime powers of exponent `1`. -/
    58	theorem prime_primePower {q : ℕ} (hqPrime : Nat.Prime q) :
    59	    ∃ p n, Nat.Prime p ∧ 0 < n ∧ q = p ^ n := by
    60	  exact ⟨q, 1, hqPrime, by decide, by simp⟩
    61	
    62	/-- Build parameters from explicit prime-power data `q = p^n`. -/
    63	def ofPrimePower (m q d p n : ℕ) (hm : 0 < m) (hp : Nat.Prime p) (hn : 0 < n)
    64	    (hq : q = p ^ n) : Parameters :=
    65	  { m := m
    66	    q := q
    67	    d := d
    68	    hm := hm
    69	    hq := q_pos_of_primePower ⟨p, n, hp, hn, hq⟩
    70	    hqPrimePower := ⟨p, n, hp, hn, hq⟩ }
    71	
    72	/-- Build parameters when `q` itself is prime. -/
    73	def ofPrime (m q d : ℕ) (hm : 0 < m) (hqPrime : Nat.Prime q) : Parameters :=
    74	  { m := m
    75	    q := q
    76	    d := d
    77	    hm := hm

    82	def ofTwo (m d : ℕ) (hm : 0 < m) : Parameters :=

    85	/-- Paper finite fields have at least two elements: `q = p^n` with `p` prime

    87	theorem two_le_q (params : Parameters) : 2 ≤ params.q := by

    89	  rw [hq]

# Mathematical Language Guidelines

MIPStarRE Lean names and documentation should be written for readers comparing
the formalization with the paper and blueprint.

This is a project-local supplement to the Mathlib-derived documentation,
naming, and style guides in the lean-conventions skill's `MATHLIB_doc`,
`MATHLIB_naming`, and `MATHLIB_style` references.

## Scope

These guidelines apply to:

- public Lean declaration names and namespace names;
- module docstrings;
- declaration docstrings;
- documentation-visible section comments;
- explanatory comments that describe the mathematical role of a declaration.
- blueprint prose and formalization-support notes;
- issue titles and issue bodies;
- PR titles and PR descriptions.

## Source of Truth

Use terminology from the following sources, in this order:

1. `references/ldt-paper/`
2. `blueprint/src/chapter/`
3. established local conventions in nearby Lean files

When the paper has a term for the object, use that term. For Section 5, for
example, prefer orthogonalization lemma, truncation function, rounding to
projectors, rank reduction, and completing to measurement.

## Reference Notation And Terminology

The notation and terminology of the original reference are the default for
reader-facing mathematical text.  A reader should be able to compare a Lean
docstring, blueprint paragraph, issue, or PR description with the cited source
without first learning a private vocabulary used by the formalization.

When Lean must use a different name or representation, define the deviation in a
location which future readers can find from the affected statement.  Use the
first applicable location in the following order:

1. the declaration docstring of the public object whose name or representation
   differs from the paper;
2. the module docstring of the defining Lean file, when the deviation concerns a
   family of declarations in that file;
3. the relevant blueprint paragraph, when the notation appears only in the
   blueprint;
4. a report under `docs/reports/` or `docs/paper-gaps/`, when the deviation is a
   larger discrepancy between the paper, blueprint, and Lean.

The explanation should say:

- the notation or term used in the paper;
- the Lean object or name which represents it;
- the mathematical reason for the difference, if there is one;
- the scope in which the replacement should be used.

A PR description may mention the deviation, but it should not be the only place
where future readers can learn it.

Formalization-only auxiliary lemmas should be introduced as such.  Their prose
should name the nearby paper equation, theorem, or construction they support,
rather than presenting the auxiliary name as paper terminology.

## Naming Norm

Names and prose should describe the mathematical object, hypothesis, or
conclusion. They should not encode the history of how the formalization was
assembled.

Avoid presenting words such as `pipeline`, `wrapper`, `package`, `raw`,
`oneShot`, or `liveBlock` as mathematical terminology unless the cited source
uses them with that meaning. Likewise, avoid implementation-local substitutes
such as `projectivization` or `spectral truncation` when the paper gives a
clearer phrase.

This is a general rule for the repository, not only a rule for file splits.
Module names, namespace names, public declarations, theorem fields, docstrings,
blueprint-facing names, issue titles, and spec documents should name the
mathematical layer under discussion, not the local workflow step, paper line
number, or implementation history.

### Concrete examples

The table below illustrates the naming norm with examples patterned on the
codebase and on names seen during review.  Some entries are existing names;
others are proposed names for future refactors.  The "avoid" column lists
process-shaped names that encode the history of how the formalization was
assembled; the "prefer" column lists mathematical names that a reader of the
paper or blueprint would recognize.

| Avoid (process-shaped)                        | Prefer (mathematical)                     | Rationale                                              |
|:----------------------------------------------|:------------------------------------------|:-------------------------------------------------------|
| `Line130`                                     | `ProjectiveConsistency`                   | Paper Lemma 5.13, not "the line-130 identity"          |
| `Line169`                                     | `CompletionTransport`                     | Paper Lemma 5.16, step that transports completed data  |
| `Step6`                                       | `Orthonormalization`                      | Paper Section 5, the orthonormalization construction   |
| `FinalAssembly`                               | `DiagonalCompletion`                      | Paper Lemma 5.17, constructing a diagonal POVM         |
| `OneShotIneq`                                 | `SelfConsistencyDataProcessing` (or existing module `Preliminaries.SelfConsistency.DataProcessing`)           | Paper's data-processing inequality for self-consistency |
| `PipelineCheck`                               | `ErrorPropagationBound` (proposed)                   | The bound that propagates error through the test       |
| `QxpLayerWrapper`                             | `ProjectivePOVMCompletion` (proposed)                | The construction from round-projectors to POVMs        |
| `RawSpectralTruncation`                       | `SpectralTruncation`                      | The paper's spectral truncation, not an "unwrapped" version |
| `AddInUStep3To5`                              | `AddInUUpperExcessMass` (proposed)                  | Paper Addendum in §U, the upper excess-mass estimate   |
| `AddInUStep12`                                | `AddInUCommutationTail` (proposed)                   | Paper Addendum in §U, the commutation tail estimate    |

An avoided name is acceptable only when the cited paper itself uses that
phrase as the mathematical name (e.g., a lemma the paper calls "Step 2").
In that case the docstring should cite the paper's phrasing.

File-split PRs are a common place where this rule matters: new leaves should be
named by the mathematical boundary they isolate, and any public declarations
exposed by the split should be reviewed under the same standard.

### Shared helpers

When the same (or nearly the same) helper declaration appears in two or
more chapter-local leaves, the copies should be consolidated into a single
shared helper in an appropriate common module.  This avoids duplication and
ensures that fixes, generalizations, or upstream replacements apply to all
call sites at once.  Issue [#1145] tracks this work across the repository.

Procedure:

1. **Confirm equivalence.**  Compare the statement of each copy.  If the
   types differ only by a chapter-specific parameterization (e.g.,
   `SubMeas (Polynomial params) ι` vs `SubMeas (Point params) ι`),
   parameterize the shared helper over that type via a `variable` or
   explicit argument.
2. **Find the right home.**  Prefer a module that is already imported by
   both call sites.  Typical candidates:
   - `MIPStarRE/LDT/Basic/` for parameter-free operators and bounds,
   - `MIPStarRE/LDT/Preliminaries/` for polynomial/field/character lemmas,
   - The highest chapter that is a common dependency of the two sites.
3. **Name mathematically.**  Give the shared helper a name that describes
   what it states, not which chapter it originally came from.
4. **Replace call sites.**  Delete the chapter-local copies and replace
   their uses with the shared helper.  A thin wrapper is allowed only when it
   preserves a paper-facing or blueprint-facing name that external readers
   need to search for; such wrappers should have a docstring or compatibility
   comment explaining why the alias exists.  Remove the wrapper once that
   paper-facing name is no longer needed for external reference.
5. **Document.**  Add a docstring to the shared helper citing the paper or
   blueprint location it supports.

### Legacy identifier treatment

If a docstring must mention a legacy Lean identifier, cite it in backticks and
describe the mathematical object in paper terminology. If an old public
identifier cannot be renamed in the current PR, record the required migration
in the issue, PR description, or an audit file under `audits/`.

Do not add an empty pass-through abbreviation merely to introduce a second
public name.  This is different from a documented public wrapper allowed in the
shared-helper procedure above: a wrapper must preserve a paper-facing or
blueprint-facing term and must say why the alias exists.

## Review Checklist

Reviewers should use this checklist when examining public names and
documentation prose.  Flag any item that fails.

- [ ] **Naming.**  Do public declaration names, namespace names, module names,
      theorem field names, and docstring prose describe a mathematical object,
      hypothesis, or conclusion?  Or do they encode the history of how the
      formalization was assembled (paper line numbers, workflow steps,
      implementation-phase labels)?
- [ ] **Source alignment.**  For the mathematical content under review, does
      the prose use the terminology in `references/ldt-paper/` or the
      blueprint?  Are process words such as `pipeline`, `wrapper`, `package`,
      `raw`, `oneShot`, or `liveBlock` used as mathematical terms when the
      source does not use them that way?
- [ ] **Deviation documented.**  If a Lean name or representation differs from
      the paper, is the deviation documented in a declaration docstring,
      module docstring, blueprint paragraph, or `docs/paper-gaps/` note, in
      that order of preference?
- [ ] **Auxiliary lemmas.**  Are formalization-only auxiliary lemmas introduced
      as such, with prose naming the nearby paper equation, theorem, or
      construction they support?
- [ ] **Shared helpers.**  Does the PR introduce a helper that already exists
      (or near-exists) in another chapter-local leaf?  If so, has it been
      consolidated into a common module with a mathematical name?
- [ ] **Legacy IDs.**  If a legacy Lean identifier is mentioned, is the
      mathematical object described in paper terminology?  If an old public
      identifier cannot be renamed yet, is the required migration recorded in
      the issue, PR description, or an audit file?
- [ ] **Pass-through names.**  Does the PR add an empty pass-through
      abbreviation that introduces a second public name without adding
      mathematical content?  Reject it unless it is a documented compatibility
      wrapper preserving paper-facing or blueprint-facing terminology.

Review-fix PRs touching a surface covered by an active audit should read the
relevant audit before changing names or prose.

    59	`CombinedPointsWitness.extendedQ`.  This is `lem:qld-4-12`, paper lines
    60	993--1011; the `XZ` and `ZX` source products remain separate. -/

    62	    {S : ProjectiveSetting P ε} (points : CombinedPointsWitness S δ) :

    70	        (fun question c => S.place p2
    71	          ((points.extendedQ p2.side question.1.1 question.1.2
    72	            question.2.1 question.2.2).effect c))

    76	        (fun question c => S.place p1
    77	          ((points.extendedQ p1.side question.1.1 question.1.2
    78	            question.2.1 question.2.2).effect c))
    79	        (fun question c => S.place p2
    80	          (∑ ab ∈ Finset.univ.filter (fun ab : PauliScalar P × PauliScalar P =>
    81	              question.2.1 * ab.1 + question.2.2 * ab.2 = c),
    82	            (S.pointMeasExp p2.side .X question.1.1).effect ab.1 *
    83	              (S.pointMeasExp p2.side .Z question.1.2).effect ab.2))
    84	        S.psiHat <= δ) ∧

    87	        (fun question c => S.place p1
    88	          ((points.extendedQ p1.side question.1.1 question.1.2

    93	            (S.pointMeasExp p2.side .Z question.1.2).effect ab.2 *
    94	              (S.pointMeasExp p2.side .X question.1.1).effect ab.1))

     7	/-!
     8	# Witnesses for combining the Pauli bases
     9	
    10	This module defines the five measurement and distribution witnesses used in
    11	the combining argument.  Every measurement is indexed by the player side, so
    12	Alice's and Bob's local spaces remain distinct.  The extended-dimensional
    13	line objects use the directly indexed low-degree interface and therefore do
    14	not require a dimension-divisibility hypothesis.
    15	
    16	## References
    17	
    18	`CombinedPointsWitness`, `CombinedLinesWitness`, and `GlobalPairWitness` record
    19	the measurement conclusions of `lem:qld-4-10`, `lem:qld-xz-lines`, and
    20	`lem:qld-4-7`, respectively, in
    21	`blueprint/src/chapter/ch15_qpbt_combining.tex`.  `SubLineWitness` and
    22	`ExtendedLinesWitness` instead support `lem:qld-sublines` and `lem:qld-4-13`
    23	through the directly indexed extended-line carrier and probability law.  The
    24	latter also uses the completed answer alphabet, rather than the field-valued
    25	answer sum in the source statement.  The paper source is
    26	`references/qpbt-paper/14_analysis_of_the_pauli_basis_test.tex:689-709,
    27	882-894,1020-1069,1267-1274`.
    28	-/

    37	/-! ## The canonical scalar identification -/
    38	
    39	/-- Identify the direct extended game's scalar field with the Pauli scalar
    40	field.  Both are selected by `fixedFieldModel`; only their proof argument for
    41	admissibility differs. -/
    42	noncomputable def extendedDirectScalarEquiv (P : AdmissibleParams) :
    43	    DirectScalarQ P.extendedDirectLd ≃+* PauliScalar P := by
    44	  have h : P.extendedDirectLd.hq = P.hq := Subsingleton.elim _ _
    45	  cases h
    46	  exact RingEquiv.refl _
    47	
    48	/-- Transport an extended direct point into the canonical Pauli scalar field. -/
    49	def directPointToPauli (P : AdmissibleParams)
    50	    (u : Fin P.extendedDirectLd.m -> DirectScalarQ P.extendedDirectLd) :
    51	    Fin (2 * P.m + 2) -> PauliScalar P :=
    52	  fun i => extendedDirectScalarEquiv P (u i)

    54	/-! ## Finite direct-line carrier -/
    55	
    56	/-- A finite code for directly indexed lines, omitting only proof fields. -/
    57	private abbrev DirectLineDescCode (D : DirectLdParams) :=
    58	  ((Fin D.m -> DirectScalarQ D) × Fin D.m) ⊕
    59	    ((Fin D.m -> DirectScalarQ D) × Fin D.m ×
    60	      (Fin D.m -> DirectScalarQ D))
    61	
    62	/-- Encode a directly indexed line by its tag and mathematical data. -/
    63	private def directLineDescCode (D : DirectLdParams) :
    64	    DirectLineDesc D -> DirectLineDescCode D
    65	  | .axis base index _ => .inl (base, index)
    66	  | .diagonal base index direction _ _ => .inr (base, index, direction)
    67	
    68	/-- The direct-line code is injective by proof irrelevance. -/
    69	private theorem directLineDescCode_injective (D : DirectLdParams) :
    70	    Function.Injective (directLineDescCode D) := by
    71	  intro line line' h
    72	  cases line with
    73	  | axis base index baseFixed =>
    74	      cases line' with
    75	      | axis base' index' baseFixed' =>
    76	          simp only [directLineDescCode, Sum.inl.injEq, Prod.mk.injEq] at h
    77	          rcases h with ⟨rfl, rfl⟩
    78	          rfl
    79	      | diagonal => simp [directLineDescCode] at h
    80	  | diagonal base index direction baseFixed prefixZero =>
    81	      cases line' with
    82	      | axis => simp [directLineDescCode] at h
    83	      | diagonal base' index' direction' baseFixed' prefixZero' =>
    84	          simp only [directLineDescCode, Sum.inr.injEq, Prod.mk.injEq] at h
    85	          rcases h with ⟨rfl, rfl, rfl⟩
    86	          rfl
    87	
    88	/-- Directly indexed line descriptions form a finite type. -/
    89	noncomputable instance directLineDescFintype (D : DirectLdParams) :
    90	    Fintype (DirectLineDesc D) :=
    91	  Fintype.ofInjective (directLineDescCode D) (directLineDescCode_injective D)

    93	/-! ## Combined point and line measurements -/
    94	
    95	/-- Projective joint point measurements and their ordered consistency
    96	guarantees from `lem:qld-4-10`, paper lines 689--709.  The `XZ` and `ZX`
    97	products are retained as distinct fields. -/
    98	structure CombinedPointsWitness {P : AdmissibleParams} {ε : ℝ}
    99	    (S : ProjectiveSetting P ε) (δ : ℝ) where
   100	  /-- The complete joint measurement on each player's expanded local space. -/
   101	  Q : (side : PlayerSide) ->
   102	    (Fin P.m -> PauliScalar P) ->
   103	    (Fin P.m -> PauliScalar P) ->
   104	    Measurement (PauliScalar P × PauliScalar P) (S.ExpandedLocalSpace side)
   105	  /-- Every joint point measurement is projective. -/
   106	  projective : ∀ side x z, Measurement.IsProjective (Q side x z)
   107	  /-- Joint point measurements agree across every directed opposite placement. -/
   108	  self_consistent : ∀ p1 p2 : Placement, p1.IsOpposite p2 ->
   109	    opFamilyDistSq
   110	      (uniformDistribution
   111	        ((Fin P.m -> PauliScalar P) × (Fin P.m -> PauliScalar P)))
   112	      (fun xz ab => S.place p1 ((Q p1.side xz.1 xz.2).effect ab))
   113	      (fun xz ab => S.place p2 ((Q p2.side xz.1 xz.2).effect ab))
   114	      S.psiHat <= δ
   115	  /-- Joint point measurements are close to the ordered `X`-then-`Z` product. -/
   116	  consistent_XZ : ∀ p1 p2 : Placement, p1.IsOpposite p2 ->
   117	    opFamilyDistSq
   118	      (uniformDistribution
   119	        ((Fin P.m -> PauliScalar P) × (Fin P.m -> PauliScalar P)))
   120	      (fun xz ab => S.place p1 ((Q p1.side xz.1 xz.2).effect ab))
   121	      (fun xz ab => S.place p2
   122	        ((S.pointMeasExp p2.side .X xz.1).effect ab.1 *
   123	          (S.pointMeasExp p2.side .Z xz.2).effect ab.2))
   124	      S.psiHat <= δ
   125	  /-- Joint point measurements are close to the ordered `Z`-then-`X` product. -/
   126	  consistent_ZX : ∀ p1 p2 : Placement, p1.IsOpposite p2 ->
   127	    opFamilyDistSq
   128	      (uniformDistribution
   129	        ((Fin P.m -> PauliScalar P) × (Fin P.m -> PauliScalar P)))
   130	      (fun xz ab => S.place p1 ((Q p1.side xz.1 xz.2).effect ab))
   131	      (fun xz ab => S.place p2
   132	        ((S.pointMeasExp p2.side .Z xz.2).effect ab.2 *
   133	          (S.pointMeasExp p2.side .X xz.1).effect ab.1))
   134	      S.psiHat <= δ
   135	
   136	/-- Joint line measurements and their evaluation consistency from
   137	`lem:qld-xz-lines`, paper lines 882--894.  Evaluation uses explicit `Option`
   138	outcomes, including the class of answers not determined at the sampled point. -/
   139	structure CombinedLinesWitness {P : AdmissibleParams} {ε δQ : ℝ}
   140	    (S : ProjectiveSetting P ε) (points : CombinedPointsWitness S δQ)
   141	    (δ : ℝ) where
   142	  /-- The complete paired-line measurement on each expanded local space. -/
   143	  T : (side : PlayerSide) ->
   144	    LineDesc P.toLdParams -> LineDesc P.toLdParams ->
   145	    Measurement
   146	      (DegPoly P.toLdParams (P.m * P.d) ×
   147	        DegPoly P.toLdParams (P.m * P.d))
   148	      (S.ExpandedLocalSpace side)
   149	  /-- On an axis-parallel X line, outcomes outside degree `d` have zero effect. -/
   150	  axis_degree_X : ∀ side lineX lineZ fX fZ,
   151	    lineX.kind = .axis -> Not (DegPoly.FitsDegree P.d fX) ->
   152	      (T side lineX lineZ).effect (fX, fZ) = 0
   153	  /-- On an axis-parallel Z line, outcomes outside degree `d` have zero effect. -/
   154	  axis_degree_Z : ∀ side lineX lineZ fX fZ,
   155	    lineZ.kind = .axis -> Not (DegPoly.FitsDegree P.d fZ) ->
   156	      (T side lineX lineZ).effect (fX, fZ) = 0
   157	  /-- Evaluated line pairs are consistent with the completed point-pair
   158	  measurement on every directed opposite placement. -/
   159	  consistent : ∀ p1 p2 : Placement, p1.IsOpposite p2 ->
   160	    consistencyDefect
   161	      (Distribution.prod (linePointDist P.toLdParams)
   162	        (linePointDist P.toLdParams))
   163	      (fun sample answer => S.place p1
   164	        (((T p1.side sample.1.1 sample.2.1).postprocess fun fs =>
   165	          (evalOpt sample.1.1 sample.1.2 fs.1,
   166	            evalOpt sample.2.1 sample.2.2 fs.2)).effect answer))
   167	      (fun sample answer => S.place p2
   168	        (((points.Q p2.side sample.1.2 sample.2.2).postprocess fun ab =>
   169	          (some ab.1, some ab.2)).effect answer))
   170	      S.psiHat <= δ
